case.display_title: Ten days of fever, abdominal pain and loose stools

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to see a 55-year-old woman with ten days of fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting, now confused, after failing outpatient antibiotics. We reviewed the Chart so far. Fever with falling platelets, a haemolytic picture and acute kidney injury has a wide differential: bacterial sepsis including enteric fever, a tropical infection, and a thrombotic microangiopathy. The single most important question is where she has been in the past year; we will take a travel and exposure history ourselves. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Take a full travel history for the past 12 months, including prophylaxis, bites and fresh-water contact
If there has been any travel to a malaria-endemic area: thick and thin films and a rapid antigen test today, repeated 12-24 hourly to three sets if negative
Blood cultures before any change of antibiotics; stool culture and parasites
Lactate, glucose, renal and liver function and a coagulation screen

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to see a woman with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia, haemolysis and acute kidney injury; the Chart now shows four weeks in Nigeria, returning two weeks ago, without antimalarial prophylaxis. Fever in a traveller back from West Africa is Plasmodium falciparum infection until proved otherwise, and her confusion and kidney injury would make it a medical emergency. This must be excluded today, before any treatment directed at a thrombotic microangiopathy. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Thick and thin films with a parasite count, and a rapid antigen test, now; repeat 12-24 hourly to three sets if negative
If parasites are seen, start artemisinin-based treatment without waiting for other results: intravenous artesunate while she is confused or vomiting
Check glucose, lactate, renal function and conscious level to grade severity
Blood cultures, as co-existing bacteraemia is possible

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now shows Plasmodium falciparum on the film. She has impaired consciousness and acute kidney injury, which are criteria for severe infection, so we advise intravenous artesunate now, for at least 24 hours and until she is alert and keeping tablets down, then a full three-day oral course of artemether-lumefantrine with fatty food. Oral treatment alone is not appropriate while she is confused and vomiting. The thrombocytopenia, haemolysis, schistocytes and low ADAMTS13 activity are explained by the infection; plasma exchange is not indicated. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Intravenous artesunate now (severe infection: impaired consciousness, vomiting, acute kidney injury); once alert and eating, complete a full oral course of artemether-lumefantrine
Parasite count every 12-24 hours until negative; glucose, renal function and counts daily
Cautious intravenous fluids; avoid fluid overload
Transfuse red cells if haemoglobin falls below about 7 g/dL; platelets only for bleeding
Notify the case to public health; chloroquine is not appropriate for infection acquired in Nigeria
Check for delayed haemolysis 2-4 weeks after artesunate

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on falling platelets and haemoglobin with haemolysis, acute kidney injury and confusion. We reviewed the Chart so far. The picture raises the question of a thrombotic microangiopathy, and a PLASMIC-type assessment may score high; but fever for ten days is unusual in immune TTP and infection must be excluded first. Before any plasma exchange we would want a blood film reviewed carefully, a travel history, and an ADAMTS13 sample taken before any plasma product is given. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Blood film reviewed today for schistocytes and for parasites or other red cell inclusions
If there has been any recent travel, thick and thin malaria films now
Send ADAMTS13 activity and antibody before any plasma or plasma exchange
Reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, DAT, coagulation screen and fibrinogen
Avoid platelet transfusion unless she bleeds

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now shows malarial parasites on the film. The haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and occasional schistocytes are explained by the parasitaemia. A positive ADAMTS13 antibody alone is not specific, and an activity well above 10% makes immune TTP very unlikely; activity is often mildly reduced in falciparum infection. We would not start plasma exchange, steroids or caplacizumab. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Treat the infection urgently, as advised by infectious diseases
No plasma exchange, steroids or caplacizumab
Red cell transfusion if haemoglobin falls below about 7 g/dL; platelets only for bleeding
Repeat counts, reticulocytes, LDH and a film as the parasitaemia clears; the platelets should recover within days
Review the lifelong microcytosis when she is well: iron studies are unreliable during acute infection

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on ten days of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting. We reviewed the Chart so far. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there are no features of a surgical abdomen or of inflammatory colitis. Diarrhoea and vomiting are common in systemic febrile illnesses, and with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia and haemolysis we think a systemic cause is more likely than a primary gut disorder. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Stool culture, Clostridioides difficile testing and stool microscopy if not already sent
Rehydrate and correct electrolytes
No endoscopy is indicated at present
Look for a systemic cause of fever, including a travel history

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to see a woman with fever and new confusion. We reviewed the Chart so far. She is drowsy and disoriented with a GCS around 14, but has no focal neurological signs and no neck stiffness. This looks like an encephalopathy of systemic illness rather than a primary brain disorder; causes to exclude include CNS infection, hypoglycaemia, sepsis and metabolic or drug causes, and a travel history is essential in any febrile encephalopathy. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Check capillary glucose now and regularly
Treat the systemic cause; urgent CT head only if the GCS falls or focal signs appear
Lumbar puncture if meningism develops or no systemic cause is found, once platelets and clotting allow
Neurological observations 4-hourly

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on acute kidney injury (creatinine about 150 umol/L) in a febrile, dehydrated woman with haemolysis and thrombocytopenia. We reviewed the Chart so far. The likeliest causes are volume depletion from vomiting and diarrhoea, with a contribution from the systemic infection and haemolysis; there is no evidence of obstruction. There is no indication for dialysis at present. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Intravenous fluids to restore volume, with a fluid balance chart
Urinalysis with microscopy and a renal ultrasound
Avoid nephrotoxins, including NSAIDs and contrast where possible
Daily renal function and potassium

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review abdominal pain. We reviewed the Chart so far. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no peritonism, and we see no surgical cause for her symptoms. Happy to review if the examination changes.
recommendations: No surgical intervention indicated
Re-refer if she develops peritonism or signs of obstruction

accepted_differential: Infective gastroenteritis (including Giardia and C. difficile)
efficient_path: Thick and thin films and rapid antigen test
Severity: GCS, glucose, lactate, renal function, parasite count
Intravenous artesunate, then a full oral course of artemether-lumefantrine; fluids; transfusion when Hb falls

secondary_findings: Confusion, vomiting, acute kidney injury and a parasitaemia of about 5% meet CDC and WHO criteria for severe infection (impaired consciousness, renal impairment, hyperparasitaemia by the CDC threshold); the treating team used oral artemether-lumefantrine, but the benchmark expects intravenous artesunate
Raised ADAMTS13 antibody (22 U/mL) with only mildly reduced ADAMTS13 activity (49.1%): not immune TTP
Lifelong microcytosis, proposed as homozygous alpha-plus thalassaemia (curator's judgement call, not in the article)
final_dx.text: Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a traveller returned from Nigeria without prophylaxis, with microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury and confusion mimicking thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

key_discriminators: travel to Nigeria without prophylaxis (H04, H05)
P. falciparum on thick and thin films
platelets recovering with antimalarial treatment alone

must_do.text: Take a travel history, including antimalarial prophylaxis
Send thick and thin blood films (or a rapid antigen test) for malaria urgently
Grade severity: conscious level, blood glucose and parasite count

Start intravenous artesunate promptly: impaired consciousness, vomiting, acute kidney injury and a parasitaemia of about 5% make this severe falciparum infection, so oral treatment alone is not enough
Rehydrate with intravenous fluids and monitor renal function
Monitor parasite counts and blood counts until the parasitaemia clears
Transfuse red cells when the haemoglobin falls to about 6-7 g/dL
Once she is alert and keeping tablets down after parenteral artesunate, complete a full oral course of artemether-lumefantrine

must_not_do.text: Start plasma exchange for presumed TTP
Give high-dose steroids, rituximab or caplacizumab for presumed TTP
Send her home again, or treat as gastroenteritis with antibiotics alone, without testing for malaria
Treat falciparum infection acquired in Nigeria with chloroquine

ground_truth.outcome: Afebrile after day 2; symptoms resolved by day 5; platelets normalised and she was discharged. At one month she was well, with haemoglobin 11.6 g/dL and haematocrit 36.7% (follow-up values kept out of play).

rubric.text: Falciparum malaria (severe or not), with the travel exposure identified
Falciparum malaria, travel exposure not cited
Malaria without the right species, or malarial haemolysis
TTP, another thrombotic microangiopathy, DIC, sepsis, enteric fever or infective gastroenteritis as the final diagnosis
Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: Ask every febrile patient about travel: the first emergency visit missed it
Fever in a traveller back from sub-Saharan Africa is falciparum malaria until thick and thin films say otherwise, and the films should be repeated if negative
Falciparum malaria causes a thrombotic microangiopathy with schistocytes, undetectable haptoglobin, AKI and confusion that can score high on PLASMIC
An ADAMTS13 antibody alone is not diagnostic; immune TTP needs activity below 10%
Impaired consciousness or renal impairment make falciparum infection severe: intravenous artesunate is preferred
Travellers visiting friends and relatives are the group least likely to take prophylaxis
ground_truth.treatment_given: Artemether-lumefantrine for four days, started on day 2 (Figure 2); two units of packed red cells; supportive care. No plasma exchange.

reports.impression: Plasmodium falciparum seen; parasitaemia 5%. Occasional schistocytes.
reports.report_text: Thick and thin films examined under oil immersion. Thick film: asexual parasites present. Thin film: small ring forms (early trophozoites) of Plasmodium falciparum, some red cells carrying two or more rings; infected red cells are not enlarged; no gametocytes or mature schizonts seen. Parasitaemia 5% of red cells. Occasional schistocytes. Platelets reduced.

reports.impression: Microcytic hypochromic red cells, occasional schistocytes and intra-erythrocytic ring forms.
reports.report_text: Red cells: microcytic and hypochromic with mild anisopoikilocytosis; occasional schistocytes. Intra-erythrocytic ring forms seen in some red cells. White cells: no significant morphological abnormality. Platelets: reduced on the film, no clumps. Comment: parasites seen; thick and thin films for species and parasite count recommended urgently.

reports.impression: Plasmodium falciparum ring forms with occasional schistocytes on a microcytic hypochromic background.
reports.report_text: Film reviewed by a haematopathologist. Microcytic hypochromic red cells with target cells absent and mild anisopoikilocytosis. Schistocytes are occasional only (well under 1% of red cells). Ring-form parasites in red cells of normal size, some cells with two rings and some rings at the cell margin, typical of Plasmodium falciparum; no gametocytes. Neutrophils show no toxic change; platelets reduced. Comment: the schistocytes are too few to support a primary thrombotic microangiopathy on their own; the parasitaemia explains the haemolysis and thrombocytopenia. Urgent parasite count and treatment advised.
reports.status_line: Final report, reviewed by a haematopathologist.

reports.report_text: PA erect chest radiograph. Heart size and mediastinal contours normal. Lungs clear; no consolidation, pleural effusion or pulmonary oedema.

reports.impression: No acute abdominal or pelvic abnormality.
reports.report_text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, portal venous phase. Liver, spleen (11 cm), pancreas, adrenal glands and kidneys normal. No bowel wall thickening, collection or free fluid. No lymphadenopathy. Bladder and pelvic organs unremarkable.

Liver normal in size and echotexture with no focal lesion. Gallbladder thin-walled without calculi; common bile duct not dilated. Spleen 11 cm, normal echotexture. Pancreas and kidneys normal. No free fluid.
Right kidney 10.8 cm and left kidney 11.1 cm, with preserved corticomedullary differentiation. No hydronephrosis or calculi. Bladder poorly filled, otherwise unremarkable.
Non-contrast CT of the head. Grey-white matter differentiation preserved. No intracranial haemorrhage, infarct, mass effect or oedema. Ventricles and sulci normal for age.
